data.plain: Treating generated result records as if a person had written them as source.

analogy.boundary: The picture stops at the card; it says nothing about whether the book itself is correct or up to date.

maps.analogy: the catalogue card copied from the book
maps.doctrine: the generated record built from a source
the hand-written source it should defer to

maps.analogy: writing on the card and quoting the card as the book
maps.doctrine: editing or citing the record as the origin

analogy.text: Writing a correction on a library catalogue card and then quoting the card as if it were the book, although the card was copied from the book and the book still says something different.

reader.counterexample: Someone edits a generated result record directly and cites it as the origin of a verdict, while the source it was built from no longer matches.
reader.does_not_prove: Keeping records tied to their sources preserves the link between them; whether the source is correct is a separate question.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings in non-secret material by manifest and content hash, so each imported copy stays tied to its original and a change to the original forces the copy to be rebuilt.

reader.governs: The relationship between a generated record and the hand-written source it comes from.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating an automatically generated summary as if it were the hand-written original, and then editing or quoting it as the source while the real source no longer matches.
reader.potential_misread: That whichever copy is in front of you, with a confident verdict on it, is the thing to edit and cite.
reader.refuses: Treating a generated result record as hand-written source.
reader.requires: Each generated record tied to its inputs by hash and rebuilt from source, never edited directly or cited as the origin.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps a generated view from outranking what it was built from, so a reader knows which file is the original and which is a copy.
